events.name: A Soup Plate
events.intro: A fourth-floor room. A dresser. One plate on it, on a stand: white, with a gold rim, far too good for the room. The old woman, Madame Honorine Aubert: "That's from the Avenue d'Été. I took it. I'm not proud. Nine years I ate at that table; every Thursday; I'd nowhere else on a Thursday. The last night, I put the plate in my bag." "Not to sell. I wanted to have been somewhere. D'you understand? Nine years, and he never knew my name. He'd pass down the table, he'd say, 'Is there enough? Have you enough?' He'd fill your glass himself. He never once said, 'And who are you?'" "I'd have liked to be asked. I'd have told him: I was a seamstress; I made the dresses his mother's friends wore to dine at that same table, forty years before. I'd have liked him to know I'd been in that room both ways."

success.text: "If I could bring something. I can still do a tart. I'd not go empty again. It's hard on a person, nine years of being given to."
She looks at it a long time. Then she wraps it in a tea towel and puts it in your hands. "Lend. Not give. It's the only thing I've got that says I was there."
"Extraordinary. That was the trouble. You can't feed four hundred people like that. You can feed four hundred people soup. He wouldn't. He'd have thought it an insult."

events.name: Enough Well
events.intro: A hamlet in the Kalos badlands. A square. A well with a stone rim and a brass plate: GIFT OF A FRIEND. Children. A queue of two, with buckets, chatting. A woman at the rope, Madame Clémence Girard: "The eleventh. That's what the man who dug it called it; he'd a number for each. Tall. Red hair. Dug with the crew, in his shirt. My husband said: a gentleman who blisters. You don't see it." "Twenty years. It's never gone dry. We've had the drought, same as the south. It went low. We queued. It was enough." "He's never been back. I'd have thought he'd want to see one that worked. You'd want to, wouldn't you? After the other."

success.text: "A village in the south. He'd dug theirs first. It went dry in the drought, and they went with it. Everybody knows. Nobody says it to him."

"It wasn't, on its own. Nobody's well is. We'd the well and a cistern we built ourselves, the second year, and a rule about gardens. He gave us the hole. We made it enough." She hauls. "He'd not have liked the cistern. It's ugly."
"He's thirty-one of these. I don't suppose he's had a letter from one. You don't write to thank a man for water. It'd be like thanking him for Tuesday."

events.name: Enough Well
events.intro: She fills a bottle. "If you see him. Tell him the eleventh's enough. And tell him why."

events.name: Page Nine
events.intro: A press. The smell of ink. A man with a loupe and a galley proof he's kept two years. The typesetter, Monsieur Fabrice Collet: "A Beautiful Future. Eleven pages, four colours, a thousand copies on the heavy stock. I set it myself. You read what you set; you can't help it. Letter by letter." "Page nine. 'The device removes the surplus.' I stopped the press. I rang the client. I said, monsieur, there's a line here I don't follow; is it a figure of speech?" "A lady came on. Very warm. She said: 'It's conceptual.' I said, ah. I ran it." He holds up the proof. In the margin of page nine, in blue pencil, a printer's mark: ? "That's a query. It means: author to confirm. It was never confirmed. I ran it with the query open. I've not done that before or since."

success.text: "I thought it meant what it said. That's the trouble with setting type. You can't not read it."
He hands it over. The blue question mark is the only thing on the page in his own hand.
"For whom?" "For anyone who's got the brochure." He thinks. He goes to the type case. "One line. Under page nine. What should it say?"

events.name: The Brother
events.intro: Geosenge. A small stone, among the big ones, set a little apart. No cable on it. Lichen. Letters almost gone. He'd no talent for kingship and he knew it; that was his talent." AZ: "When I built the machine, he came to the door of the workshop. He said: 'Brother, what does it eat?' I said: nothing you'll miss. He said: 'Then it eats something.' He didn't come in." AZ: "He raised this himself. For the ones I took. He never told me. I found it six hundred years on. events.name: The Other Column
events.intro: Lumiose: the Prefecture. A records office. Ledgers to the ceiling. A woman on a rolling ladder. The census clerk, Mademoiselle Séverine Moreau: "He came himself. Six years ago. Very courteous; he held the ladder. He wanted the figures for the south: villages, head by head. I gave them." "He came back every spring. Same request. The count. It went up; it does. He'd go quite white. He'd say: 'More.'" "He only ever asked for the one column. I've two. I said, the third year. I said, monsieur, would you like the other? He said, 'What other?' I said: what they grew. He said he'd not time." She turns the ledger. Two columns. Heads. And beside it: yield. Hectares under the plough. Cisterns. Schools. The second column's gone up faster than the first. Every year but one. "The drought year. That's the one he looked at. I don't blame him; it's a dreadful year. But it's one. He's built on one year and one column."
